redteam_bye_fade_sham_placebo_null.plain_summary: Placebo: this fakes each team's bye week by randomly shifting it one or two weeks off from where it actually fell, then reruns the exact same 'fade the team coming off a bye' bet on those fictional bye weeks, repeated 100 times. Since the bye weeks used here aren't real, any effect this finds is noise the method invents on its own; it came back close to zero, which supports treating the real bye-week finding elsewhere in this registry as a genuine pattern rather than an artifact of the method.

redteam_bye_overval_fade_full_slate_with.plain_summary: A team is coming off its bye week. This re-tests the bet against that team using a corrected way of identifying bye weeks that avoids a bug which had been mislabeling every season-opening game as coming off a bye. The limited data leaned toward the bet working, and this result is a bug-fixed re-run of an existing bye-week finding elsewhere in this registry rather than independent new evidence.

redteam_nflcom_out2_nonstarters_only.plain_summary: A team has at least two players officially listed as Out for Friday's injury report, but none of them are regular starters, a decomposition built to check whether an existing 'multiple players Out' finding depends on losing depth players or on losing starters. This is the depth-players-only half of that check, and the limited data leaned only weakly and inconclusively toward hurting that team, unlike the starters-only half, which is a stronger, separate finding elsewhere in this registry.

redteam_nflcom_out2_starters_only.plain_summary: A team has at least two players officially listed as Out for Friday's injury report, and at least two of them are regular starters who played at least half their team's snaps the week before, a decomposition built to check whether an existing 'multiple players Out' finding is really about losing starters rather than just losing bodies. It leaned very strongly toward hurting that team's chances, confirming that losing starters, not just roster depth, drives the underlying finding, though this is itself a decomposition of that existing finding rather than independent new evidence.

redteam_overlay_subset_loso_cv.plain_summary: Not a bet on any single game: this is a robustness check on how the model chooses which combination of overlay adjustments to use, by picking the best-looking combination from five seasons of data and then testing that fixed choice on a sixth season it never saw, repeated one held-out season at a time. The result came back essentially a coin flip, which undercuts an earlier, more optimistic expectation for how much this piece of the model should be worth.

redzone_reversion_c1_rz_over_fade.plain_summary: A team scored touchdowns unusually often once it reached the red zone last season, among the league's best quarter, on the idea that unusually hot red-zone scoring tends to cool off the next season. This was tested as a bet against that team the following season, and the limited data came back essentially a coin flip, while the underlying red-zone-scoring tendency itself was found to carry over only weakly from one season to the next, undercutting the premise.

redzone_reversion_c2_rz_under_rebound.plain_summary: A team scored touchdowns unusually rarely once it reached the red zone last season, among the league's worst quarter, on the idea that unusually cold red-zone scoring tends to bounce back the next season. This was tested as a bet on that team the following season, and the limited data leaned away from the idea.

redzone_reversion_c3_third_down_over_fad.plain_summary: A team converted third downs unusually often last season, among the league's best quarter, on the idea that an unusually hot third-down conversion rate tends to cool off the next season. This was tested as a bet against that team the following season, and the limited data leaned strongly toward the idea, the strongest lean among a related group of red-zone and third-down reversion checks.

redzone_reversion_c4_third_down_under_re.plain_summary: A team converted third downs unusually rarely last season, among the league's worst quarter, on the idea that an unusually cold third-down conversion rate tends to bounce back the next season. This was tested as a bet on that team the following season, and the limited data leaned against the idea, though it stayed just short of ruling it out.

redzone_reversion_c5_hot_offense_vs_stin.plain_summary: The visiting team had an unusually hot red-zone scoring offense last season while the home team's defense was unusually poor at stopping red-zone touchdowns last season, a matchup expected to fade back toward average and favor the home team. This was tested as a bet on the home team, on 234 qualifying games, and the limited data leaned toward the idea.

redzone_reversion_c6_early_season_extrem.plain_summary: In the first half of the season, weeks 1 through 8, a team was among the league's best quarter last season in either red-zone scoring or third-down conversion (or both), on the idea that an extreme prior-season strength fades especially early, before a new season's true form is visible. This was tested as a bet against that team, and the limited data leaned away from the idea.

referee_battery_home_penalty_tilt_bottom.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game was, last season, among the least likely refs to call more penalties on the visiting team than the home team, the bottom quarter of that tendency. This was tested as a bet on the home team anyway, and while the limited data leaned toward the idea, the referee's own penalty-calling tendency was found to barely carry over from one season to the next, which undercuts the idea that any individual referee has a persistent, predictable bias at all.

referee_battery_home_penalty_tilt_top_qu.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game was, last season, among the most likely refs to call more penalties on the visiting team than the home team, on the idea that a referee's own history of favoring the home team with penalty calls might persist. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and while the limited data leaned toward the idea, the referee's own penalty-calling tendency was found to barely carry over from one season to the next, which undercuts the idea that any individual referee has a persistent, predictable bias at all.

referee_battery_penalty_rate_bottom_quar.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game called an unusually low total number of penalties per game last season, among the league's bottom quarter of refs by that measure, on the idea that a low-flag game disrupts the road team's offense less than usual. This was tested as a bet against the home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, with the referee's overall penalty rate itself shown to carry over moderately from one season to the next.

referee_battery_penalty_rate_top_quartil.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game called an unusually high total number of penalties per game last season, among the league's top quarter of refs by that measure, on the idea that a high-flag game disrupts the road team's offensive rhythm and communication more than the home team's. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, with the referee's overall penalty rate itself shown to carry over moderately from one season to the next.

referee_battery_rookie_home_cover.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game is working their first season as a head referee on record, on the idea that a less experienced official might be more swayed by a loud home crowd. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and the limited data came back essentially an exact coin flip.

referee_battery_veteran_home_cover.plain_summary: The head referee assigned to this game has worked at least five prior seasons as a head referee, on the idea that a veteran official is less swayed by a loud home crowd than a rookie one, producing a smaller home-field advantage in their games. This was tested as a bet against the home team relative to the rest of the slate, and the limited data leaned away from the idea.

residual_location_purged_cv_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether a specific piece of the model's probability-calibration machinery, the exact center-point of its error distribution rather than just which way the error leans, adds value, using an alternative testing method the project doesn't normally use (called purged cross-validation) instead of its usual week-by-week evaluation. The limited data leaned slightly against this piece of machinery adding value, but a related test of the same question using the project's normal evaluation method came out with the opposite point estimate, and neither one is resolved, so the two should not be averaged together as if they were the same measurement.

residual_location_recency_hl100_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether weighting the model's recent errors more heavily than older ones, with a fast, roughly 100-game fade-out, when calibrating its probabilities beats treating all past errors equally the way the model currently does. The limited data leaned away from this weighting change helping.

residual_location_recency_hl200_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether weighting the model's recent errors more heavily than older ones, fading out over roughly 200 games, when calibrating its probabilities beats treating all past errors equally the way the model currently does. The limited data leaned away from this weighting change helping, though the result stops short of ruling it out.

residual_location_recency_hl400_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether weighting the model's recent errors more heavily than older ones, fading out over roughly 400 games, when calibrating its probabilities beats treating all past errors equally the way the model currently does. The limited data leaned away from this weighting change helping; every version of this same weighting idea tried at different fade-out speeds leaned the same losing direction on the same games, though that pattern alone isn't treated as a fresh, independent finding since they all share the same games and mechanism.

residual_location_recency_hl800_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether weighting the model's recent errors more heavily than older ones, fading out very slowly over roughly 800 games, when calibrating its probabilities beats treating all past errors equally the way the model currently does. The limited data leaned away from this weighting change helping.

residual_location_shrink_025_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether pulling the center-point of the model's error distribution 25% of the way toward zero, a more conservative calibration setting, beats the model's current setting. The limited data came back close to a coin flip, leaning only slightly away from the change helping.

residual_location_shrink_050_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether pulling the center-point of the model's error distribution halfway toward zero, a more conservative calibration setting, beats the model's current setting. The limited data leaned away from the change helping.

residual_location_shrink_075_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether pulling the center-point of the model's error distribution 75% of the way toward zero, a more conservative calibration setting, beats the model's current setting. The limited data leaned away from the change helping.

residual_location_shrink_100_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether removing the center-point of the model's error distribution entirely, forcing it to assume its errors average out to exactly zero, beats the model's current, less extreme calibration setting. The limited data leaned away from the change helping.

residual_location_train_recency_hl100_cf.plain_summary: College football: this is a model-settings test, not a bet on any game -- it checks whether weighting the games used to originally train the model's scoring formula more heavily toward recent games, fading out over roughly 100 games, beats training on all past games equally, isolating that idea from a related, already-tested one about weighting errors after training rather than the training data itself. The limited data leaned away from this training-weighting change helping.

forecast_weather_kn_temp_swing_prior_wee.plain_summary: The visiting team faces a forecast temperature swing of 30 degrees or more compared with the actual weather at their own previous game, in an outdoor stadium -- a shock that only the visiting team has to adjust to. Bet on the home team; the limited data leans toward the idea across the 2009-2025 seasons.

The visiting team faces a forecast temperature swing of 30 degrees or more compared with the actual weather at their own previous game, in an outdoor stadium, checked only across the 2009-2019 seasons. Bet on the home team; the limited data from that earlier period leans toward the idea.

forecast_weather_kn_warm_team_cold_late_.plain_summary: A team that normally plays its home games in a warm-winter city is on the road late in the season (week 13 or later) for an outdoor game forecast at 35 degrees or colder -- real winter cold a warm-climate team rarely has to handle. Bet on the home team; the limited data leans toward the idea across the 2009-2025 seasons, using the weather forecast closest to kickoff.

A team that normally plays its home games in a warm-winter city is on the road late in the season (week 13 or later) for an outdoor game forecast at 35 degrees or colder, checked only across the 2009-2019 seasons using the weather forecast closest to kickoff. Bet on the home team; the limited data from that period leans toward the idea.

forecast_weather_kn_wind_passing_away_fa.plain_summary: The visiting team is favored to win, throws the ball more than almost any other team in the league, and is heading into an outdoor game with forecast wind of 15 miles per hour or more -- conditions that in theory disrupt a pass-heavy game plan. Tested as a bet on the home underdog across the 2009-2025 seasons, and the limited data leaned slightly against the idea.

The visiting team is favored to win, throws the ball more than almost any other team in the league, and is heading into an outdoor game with forecast wind of 15 miles per hour or more, checked only across the 2009-2019 seasons. Tested as a bet on the home underdog, and the limited data from that period leaned toward the idea.

forecast_weather_temp_gap_cold_visitor.plain_summary: The visiting team's home climate runs at least 25 degrees warmer on average than the pregame forecast for today's outdoor game -- a genuine weather forecast made days ahead, not a look back at the actual game-day temperature. This is one of four related weather checks tried together; bet on the home team, and the limited data leaned strongly toward the idea across the 2020-2025 seasons for which forecast data exists.

forecast_weather_warm_team_cold_late.plain_summary: A team that normally plays its home games in a warm-winter city is on the road late in the season (week 13 or later), and the pregame weather forecast made the Tuesday before kickoff -- genuinely available before the pool's picks lock -- calls for an outdoor game at 35 degrees or colder. This is one of four related weather checks tried together; bet on the home team, and the limited data leaned strongly toward the idea across the 2020-2025 seasons for which forecast data exists.

fourth_down_aggressiveness.plain_summary: A team's head coach has been going for it on fourth down more often than the situation statistically called for, based on the prior season's tendency. This one is measured on a different scale than most rules on this page -- in average scoring-margin points against the spread, not in pick-accuracy percentage -- and the limited data came back close to even.

graph_schedule_rating_brier.plain_summary: This tests adding team-strength ratings computed the same way search engines rank web pages -- treating each week's schedule as a network of who-beat-whom and finding the most influential teams in it -- as extra ingredients in the model's market-comparison features. It's measured on how well the model's stated probabilities matched reality (a calibration score, not the usual pick-accuracy percentage), and no supporting data file survives from when this was originally run, only a written note; the limited data leaned away from the idea.

groupwise_ridge_block_penalties.plain_summary: College football: this tests applying a different amount of statistical smoothing to different groups of the model's input columns -- lighter smoothing on well-established betting-market numbers, heavier smoothing on thinner player-level stats -- instead of one single smoothing setting for everything. At the smoothing level the model actually uses in production this change makes almost no difference either way, so it was shelved rather than adopted, even though the limited data leaned toward it helping.

hc_year_one_fade.plain_summary: A team is playing under a head coach in their first season with them, in weeks 1 through 8. Bet against that team. First-year coaches cover 46.7% of the time; coaches held over from last season cover 51.0%.

illness_away_active_ge1.plain_summary: At least one player on the visiting team is carrying a team-reported illness designation (flu or sickness, not a season-ending injury), though still expected to play. Bet on the home team; the limited data leans toward the idea. This is one of several related illness-count checks built together, using injury-report data confirmed to closely match the league's own designations.

illness_away_ge2.plain_summary: At least two players on the visiting team are carrying a team-reported illness designation heading into the game. Bet on the home team; the limited data leans toward the idea. This is one of several related illness-count checks built together, using injury-report data confirmed to closely match the league's own designations.

illness_differential_home_worse.plain_summary: Narrowed to games where sickness is lopsided -- one team has two or more players carrying an illness designation while the other has at most one -- this compares what happens when the home team is the sicker side against when the away team is the sicker side. The hypothesis was that home-field advantage suffers when the home team is the sicker one, so bet against that home team; the limited data, drawn from a small sample of only 214 such games, leaned toward the idea.

illness_home_active_ge1.plain_summary: At least one player on the home team is carrying a team-reported illness designation heading into the game, though still expected to play. This was tested as a bet against that home team, and the limited data leaned away from the idea. This is one of several related illness-count checks built together, using injury-report data confirmed to closely match the league's own designations.

illness_home_ge2.plain_summary: At least two players on the home team are carrying a team-reported illness designation heading into the game. This was tested as a bet against that home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea. This is one of several related illness-count checks built together, using injury-report data confirmed to closely match the league's own designations.

injury_value_lost_gradient.plain_summary: Splitting games into three equal groups by how much total player value was lost to injury (weighing not just how many players were out but how important they were), games in the top third for value lost covered notably more than games in the bottom third: -0.66 points below baseline in the lowest-loss third, +0.66 in the middle third, and +5.26 in the highest-loss third. This isolates which games actually drive the edge in an injury-value feature already built into the live model.

injury_value_lost_narrowed.plain_summary: A cleaner version of a total-injury-value-lost measure, built to strip out a separate modeling choice (how quickly a player's injury-report status is assumed to translate into missed snaps) so what's left measures only how much player value was actually lost to injury. Tested against the model's existing setup on a shared 456-game sample also used by several closely related injury checks, so it isn't independent evidence on its own; the limited data leaned toward the idea helping accuracy.

injury_value_lost_prior_week_absence.plain_summary: Instead of using this week's injury report (not fully visible until later in the week), this builds an injury-value estimate purely from which key players simply didn't play any snaps in their team's game the week before -- information that is fully available by the Tuesday deadline a forced-pick pool actually uses. Tested on a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, so it isn't independent evidence on its own; the limited data leaned slightly away from this Tuesday-safe substitute carrying real value.

injury_value_lost_prior_week_absence_sat.plain_summary: Not a bet on any single game: this measures the gap between what an injury-value signal could earn using each week's real injury information as of Saturday, close to kickoff, versus what it earns using only a Tuesday-visible substitute built from the previous week's missed snaps. On a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, the limited data leaned toward a substantial gap existing, meaning much of the edge depends on late information.

injury_value_lost_prior_week_report.plain_summary: Instead of this week's injury report, this builds an injury-value estimate from last week's Friday injury report, keeping only players who were flagged and then recorded zero snaps in that prior game -- information that would have been fully visible by this week's Tuesday deadline. Tested on a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, so it isn't independent evidence on its own; the limited data leaned slightly away from this Tuesday-safe substitute carrying real value.

injury_value_lost_prior_week_report_satu.plain_summary: Not a bet on any single game: this measures the gap between what an injury-value signal could earn using each week's real injury information as of Saturday versus using only a substitute built from last week's Friday injury report, which would already be visible by Tuesday. On a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, the limited data leaned toward a real gap existing, meaning a meaningful share of the edge depends on late information.

injury_value_lost_tuesday_cutoff_officia.plain_summary: This rebuilds the injury-value signal using only the league's own official injury report, checking what it would look like if a pick had to lock in at Tuesday noon rather than closer to kickoff. In practice, fewer than half a percent of the official report's entries are actually updated that early, so this version is close to using no injury information at all, and the limited data came back close to even. Tested on a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, so it isn't independent evidence on its own.

injury_value_lost_tuesday_cutoff_pft_aug.plain_summary: This rebuilds the injury-value signal for a Tuesday-noon pick deadline, supplementing the league's slow-to-update official report with football-news coverage from a sports media outlet, which roughly triples how many injury updates are actually visible in time -- though it still misses the large majority of the week's designations. Tested on a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks; the limited data leaned away from this early-visible information carrying real value.

injury_value_lost_tuesday_saturday_chann.plain_summary: Not a bet on any single game: this measures how much of an injury-value signal's backtested edge comes from information that only becomes available between a Tuesday-noon pick deadline and the following Saturday, using the league's official injury report alone as the Tuesday-visible baseline. On a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, the limited data leaned strongly toward most of the edge living in that late-arriving information, meaning it is not actually usable by a pick that has to lock on Tuesday.

Not a bet on any single game: this is the primary measurement of how much of an injury-value signal's backtested edge comes from information that only becomes available between a Tuesday-noon pick deadline and the following Saturday, using both the league's official report and football-news coverage as the Tuesday-visible baseline. On a shared 456-game sample also used by several related injury checks, the limited data leaned strongly toward essentially all of the signal's measured edge living in information that doesn't exist yet by the time a forced Tuesday pick has to be made.

interim_hc_active.plain_summary: A team is currently playing under an interim head coach after firing its coach mid-season, a spot where some believe a jolt of new motivation lifts performance against the spread. Tested as a bet on that team, and the limited data leaned slightly against the idea.

interim_hc_active_era_2009_2017.plain_summary: A team is currently playing under an interim head coach after a mid-season firing, checked only across the 2009-2017 seasons. Tested as a bet on that team, and the limited data from that era leaned slightly against the idea, in a sample too small to read with much confidence.

interim_hc_active_era_2018_2025.plain_summary: A team is currently playing under an interim head coach after a mid-season firing, checked only across the 2018-2025 seasons. Tested as a bet on that team, and the limited data from that era came back essentially dead even, in a sample too small to read with much confidence.

interim_hc_active_excl_suspension.plain_summary: A team is currently playing under an interim head coach after a mid-season firing, with one specific case removed from the data: the 2012 New Orleans Saints, whose regular coach was suspended for the season during the Bounty Scandal rather than fired, so it doesn't really fit the 'firing' story being tested. Tested as a bet on that team, and the limited data leaned slightly against the idea, essentially unchanged by removing that one case.

interim_hc_fired_year_one.plain_summary: Narrowed to interim-coach situations where the fired coach had only been on the job for one season themselves -- a firing that looks more like organizational panic than a considered reset. The idea being tested was that this kind of chaotic firing weakens any motivational lift the interim coach's team gets; the limited data came back close to a coin flip.

interim_hc_first_game.plain_summary: A team is playing its very first game under a brand-new interim head coach, right after a mid-season firing -- a sharper version of the general 'new coach bump' idea, testing only the single freshest game. Bet on that team; the limited data leaned toward the idea.

interim_hc_home_within_interim.plain_summary: Among games where either team is currently playing under an interim head coach, this simply asks whether the home team or the road team covers more often, without predicting an answer in advance -- a descriptive look rather than a themed bet. The limited data leaned toward the home team covering more in these games, in line with a normal home-field edge.

learned_availability_ats_2018_2025.plain_summary: This tests one of the model's own internal settings: whether to use a fixed, hand-set assumption for how often a given injury-report status actually keeps a player off the field, or to let the model learn that rate from the data instead, graded at the closing line from 2018 to 2025. It shares its game sample with other related model-setting checks, so it isn't independent evidence on its own; the limited data leaned mildly toward the learned version.

maxev_full_stack.plain_summary: Not a bet on a single situation: this tests stacking four separate betting rules together across the whole slate at once -- the production model's picks, a market-movement follow rule, a rule fading teams with several players ruled out, and a pressure-mismatch rule -- compared with using the model alone. Adding every rule together actually did worse than using just the two best of them together, so the project's takeaway from this test was to keep the model plus the movement rule only, not the full four-rule stack.

mexico_city_neutral.plain_summary: Regular-season games played at Mexico City's Estadio Azteca, over 7,300 feet above sea level -- one of the most extreme home-field environments in the league. Only four such games exist in the data, far too small a sample to draw any real conclusion from, and the limited data leaned slightly against the home team.

mod06_js_shrinkage_position_prior_cfb.plain_summary: College football: this tests a more refined statistical technique for estimating a new player-value feature -- instead of assuming an unproven stat is simply zero until enough games accumulate, it pulls uncertain estimates toward what's typical for a player at that position. Only the offensive side of this feature could actually be tested (the defensive-side version wasn't yet built into the model), and the limited data leaned away from the more refined technique improving accuracy.

mod06_position_prior_shrinkage.plain_summary: This tests whether the model's two player-injury-value features should be nudged toward a typical value for a player in that role, instead of toward zero, when there isn't much data yet on a specific player. Tested head to head against the model actually in production with everything else held identical, the limited data came back close to even, in a small sample too thin to read with confidence.

mod07_holdover_bias_replication.plain_summary: This checks a claim from outside betting research: that favorites who made the playoffs the year before and return largely intact come out flat in their Week 1 game, covering only 35.6% of the time historically. No supporting file survives to show exactly how this was originally computed, only a written note, and the small sample re-measured here did not confidently reproduce anything close to that extreme a number.

mod07_opener_bias_ablation.plain_summary: This measures how much three specific schedule-based adjustments -- fading playoff teams returning largely intact in Week 1, accounting for how a team did against the spread the prior week, and correcting for an early-season anchoring effect -- together contribute inside the model that is already live in production. One of the three (the playoff-holdover fade) has separately been shown not to hold up at the size originally claimed for it, so this bundled number may overstate what the group of three is really worth; the limited data on the bundle itself came back close to even.

mod08_smooth_cdf_mapping.plain_summary: This tests a different mathematical method for converting the model's raw prediction into a win/cover probability -- fitting a smooth bell-curve shape to the model's past errors, instead of the production method's more literal, step-by-step reading of those same past errors. Checked on seasons not already reserved for other tests, this alternate method also came out ahead on two separate measures of how well its stated probabilities matched reality, and the limited pick-accuracy data leaned toward switching, though not by enough on its own to change the model's default method.

mod08_smooth_cdf_mapping_opener.plain_summary: A second look at a different mathematical method for converting the model's raw prediction into a win/cover probability -- fitting a smooth bell-curve shape to past model errors instead of the production method's more literal reading of them -- this time graded at the opening line, the project's primary yardstick. The two methods never actually disagreed on which side to pick in any of the 1,537 games tested here because the comparison rule used doesn't call the probability calculation at all, but on separate measures of how well the stated probabilities matched reality, the smoother method still came out ahead.

mod11_calibration_by_regime_line_bucket.plain_summary: College football: this tests giving the model a separate probability-correction curve for different ranges of point spread -- correcting small spreads separately from big ones -- instead of one single correction curve for every game. All three correction methods tried leaned toward this being a worse approach than the single pooled curve already in use.

mod11_calibration_by_regime_season_era.plain_summary: College football: this tests giving the model a separate probability-correction curve for different eras of the sport, rather than one single correction curve applied across all seasons from 2006 to 2025. The correction methods tried leaned toward this being a modest improvement, but a separate check of whether that improvement is a stable, repeatable pattern found no consistency across the only two eras that could be compared -- too small a check to trust either way.

motivation_ladder_elim_visitor_alive_hos.plain_summary: The visiting team has been mathematically eliminated from playoff contention while the home team is still alive, in weeks 13 through 18 of the season -- a spot where a team with nothing left to play for visits one that still has something on the line. Bet on the home team; the limited data came back essentially a coin flip.

motivation_ladder_fighter_vs_nothing.plain_summary: A team still fighting for the last playoff spot faces an opponent that has nothing left to play for. The idea being tested was that the motivated team should have an edge; the main way of measuring this actually came out entirely on the opposite side of zero, a result strong enough that the project is weighing whether to call this idea disproved outright, but a second, backup way of measuring it didn't confirm that as cleanly, so no final call has been made yet.

motivation_ladder_locked_seed_wk16_18.plain_summary: A team has already clinched its playoff seed and can no longer move up or down in the standings, in weeks 16 through 18 -- the classic spot where a team might be expected to rest starters and play down to its opponent. The data actually leaned the opposite way from that prediction, with teams in this locked-in spot covering more often, not less, though the result remains inconclusive.

motivation_ladder_tank_zone_wk14_18.plain_summary: A team has one of the two worst records in the league, deep in position to land the first overall draft pick, in weeks 14 through 18 -- the spot where bettors sometimes fade a team on the idea it will roll over with nothing to play for. The data actually leaned strongly the opposite way, with these bottom-of-the-league teams covering more than expected in this stretch, not less, though the result remains inconclusive at this evaluator's resolution.

movement_attribution_pop_threshold_attri.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking only at games where the line moved by at least a point between the opening and closing lines and a specific cause for that move -- like injury news or heavy public betting -- could be identified. It shares its underlying games with a related full-slate look at following all line movement, so it isn't independent evidence; in this small sample of 168 games, the limited data leaned toward following the line being especially accurate when a cause could be pinned down.

movement_attribution_pop_threshold_injur.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking only at games where the line moved by at least a point and that move could specifically be traced to injury news. It shares its underlying games with a related full-slate look at following all line movement, so it isn't independent evidence; in this small sample of 123 games, the limited data leaned strongly toward injury-driven line moves being an especially accurate signal to follow.

movement_attribution_pop_threshold_publi.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking only at games where the line moved by at least a point and that move could specifically be traced to heavy public betting on one side. It shares its underlying games with a related full-slate look at following all line movement, so it isn't independent evidence; in this very small sample of 58 games, the limited data leaned slightly against public-driven line moves being a reliable signal to follow.

Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, narrowed further to games where a public-money-driven line move looked specifically like a sportsbook deliberately shading its price against the popular side rather than adjusting toward new information. In this tiny sample of only 29 games, the result is close to a coin flip and too small to draw any real conclusion from.

Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, narrowed further to games showing reverse line movement -- where the line moved against the side most of the public was betting on, a pattern bettors sometimes read as a sign of sharp, well-informed money. In this tiny sample of only 27 games, the limited data leaned against this specific pattern being an especially accurate signal to follow, though the sample is far too small to trust either way.

movement_attribution_pop_threshold_unatt.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking only at games where the line moved by at least a point but no specific cause -- injury news, public betting, weather -- could be identified for the move. In this sample of 122 games, the limited data leaned toward following even unexplained line movement still being a reasonably accurate signal.

movement_attribution_pop_threshold_weath.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking only at the small number of games where the line's movement could be traced specifically to weather. In this very small sample of just 24 games, the limited data leaned strongly against weather-driven line moves being a reliable signal to follow, though a sample this size cannot really settle the question.

movement_attribution_pop_unfiltered_attr.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking at every game with any observed line movement at all, however small, where a specific cause for that move -- like injury news or heavy public betting -- could be identified. It shares its underlying games with a related full-slate look at following all line movement, so it isn't independent evidence; in this sample of 257 games, the limited data leaned toward following the line being especially accurate when a cause could be pinned down.

movement_attribution_pop_unfiltered_inju.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking at every game with any observed line movement where that move could specifically be traced to injury news. It shares its underlying games with a related full-slate look at following all line movement, so it isn't independent evidence; in this sample of 185 games, the limited data leaned strongly toward injury-driven line moves being an especially accurate signal to follow.

movement_attribution_pop_unfiltered_publ.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking at every game with any observed line movement that could specifically be traced to heavy public betting on one side. In this sample of 90 games, the result came back close to a coin flip.

Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, narrowed further to games where a public-money-driven line move looked specifically like a sportsbook deliberately shading its price against the popular side rather than adjusting toward new information. In this small sample of 44 games, the result came back essentially exactly even.

Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, narrowed further to games showing reverse line movement -- where the line moved against the side most of the public was betting on, a pattern bettors sometimes read as a sign of sharp, well-informed money. In this small sample of 44 games, the limited data leaned mildly toward this pattern being a useful signal, but not strongly.

movement_attribution_pop_unfiltered_unat.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking at every game with any observed line movement where no specific cause could be identified for the move. In this sample of 237 games, the limited data leaned mildly toward following even unexplained line movement being a somewhat accurate signal.

movement_attribution_pop_unfiltered_weat.plain_summary: Not a bet on its own: this is a diagnostic slice of a broader 'follow the direction the betting line moved' rule, looking at every game with any observed line movement that could be traced specifically to weather. In this small sample of 39 games, the limited data leaned against weather-driven line moves being a reliable signal to follow.

movement_direction_tilt_opener.plain_summary: This tests overriding the model's own pick with a separate forecast of which way the betting line itself is about to move, but only when that movement forecast disagrees with the main model's pick and is relatively confident about the direction, built using only information genuinely available before each game. Tested against not overriding at all, the limited data leaned against this override helping, measured at the opening line the project treats as its main test.

movement_direction_tilt_opener_variant1_.plain_summary: This tests a more aggressive version of overriding the model's own pick with a separate forecast of which way the betting line is about to move: flipping to the movement-predicted side on every single disagreement with no confidence requirement at all, using only information genuinely available before each game. Tested against not overriding at all, the limited data leaned against this override helping, measured at the opening line the project treats as its main test.

movement_direction_tilt_opener_variant2_.plain_summary: This tests a stricter version of overriding the model's own pick with a separate forecast of which way the betting line is about to move: flipping to the movement-predicted side only on the small number of disagreements where that forecast is very confident, using only information genuinely available before each game. Tested against not overriding at all, the result came back almost exactly even, in a sample too small (only 22 flipped picks) to read with much confidence.

movement_rule_composed_chain.plain_summary: Not fully playable as described: this measures what happens if you take the production model's full chain of rules -- its base pick, adjusted for a coach-fade rule, then adjusted again for a player-arrests rule -- and then also follow whichever way the betting line actually ended up moving by kickoff, information that, by definition, isn't known until much closer to the game than the pool's Tuesday lock allows. Layered on top of that full existing chain, the limited data leaned toward this look-ahead move-following addition being a further improvement.

nflcom_friday_new_saturday_designation.plain_summary: This is not really a finding but a check on how much new injury information the league's Friday/Saturday injury report page adds beyond a separate Tuesday-updated data feed: it turns out almost every team on a given week's slate (98%) ends up with some questionable-or-worse designation by the weekend that wasn't yet showing up Tuesday, so the flag barely distinguishes any games from any others. It's an instrument-construction check, not a playable rule, and no meaningful betting conclusion can be drawn from it.

nflcom_friday_out_count_ge2.plain_summary: A team has two or more players officially ruled Out for the game, according to the league's own Friday/Saturday injury report, restricted to starter-level players (at least half of the previous week's snaps). This was tested as a bet against that short-handed team, with the direction predeclared before the data was seen, and the limited data leaned strongly toward the idea, consistently in the same direction across three separate multi-year slices of the data.

nflcom_friday_q_or_worse_starter_caliber.plain_summary: A team has at least one starter-level player (someone who played at least half of last week's snaps) listed as Questionable, Doubtful, or Out on the league's Friday/Saturday injury report. The plan, set before the data was checked, was to bet against that team; the actual measured result came out in the opposite direction from what was predicted, so this check does not support fading teams with only one such player involved.

nflcom_refresh_net_out_diff_ge1_on_chain.plain_summary: This tests adding one more layer to the production model's chain of rules: fading the team that has at least one more Out-designated player than its opponent, according to a refreshed Friday injury-report scrape, on top of everything the model already does. Compared with the existing chain of rules without this addition, the limited data leaned mildly toward the addition helping, measured at the opening line.

nflcom_refresh_out1_starter_on_chain.plain_summary: This tests adding one more layer to the production model's chain of rules: fading the team that has at least one starter-caliber player (top half of snap share) listed as Out, according to a refreshed Friday injury-report scrape, on top of everything the model already does. Compared with the existing chain of rules without this addition, the limited data leaned toward the addition helping, measured at the opening line.

bias_battery_three_plus_road_games.plain_summary: A team is playing its third or more consecutive true road game this season, without a home game in between -- an extended road trip. This was tested as a bet against that team, one of seventeen situational checks tried together in a batch, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, similarly in both halves of the period studied.

bias_battery_west_coast_early_kickoff.plain_summary: A Pacific-time-zone team (Seattle, San Francisco, the Rams, the Chargers, or the Raiders) is traveling to play a non-Pacific-time host, with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern time -- an early body-clock disadvantage for the traveling team. This was tested as a bet against that traveling team, one of seventeen situational checks tried together in a batch, and the limited data leaned toward the idea in both halves of the period studied.

bias_battery_west_coast_early_kickoff_op.plain_summary: A Pacific-time-zone team is traveling to play a non-Pacific-time host with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern time -- an early body-clock disadvantage for the traveling team. This re-checks that same situation using the odds available when betting lines first opened rather than the final lines before kickoff; the project records repeats like this only to track direction and allow later pooling, not as a standalone finding. The limited data came back close to a coin flip under this opening-line grading.

body_clock_east_host_west_visitor_early.plain_summary: An Eastern-time-zone home team is hosting a visitor based in a Western time zone, with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern -- predicted to give the home team a body-clock edge. This was tested as a bet on that home team, and of all the related body-clock checks in this registry, this is the one where the data leaned hardest against the prediction, though the measured range still just touches a coin flip at one end. It should not be pooled together with the closely related body-clock checks in this registry as if it were independent evidence.

body_clock_night_dose_1300.plain_summary: This entry was meant to test how a body-clock effect changes for games starting before 1:00 PM Eastern, but a data bug caused it to just copy the numbers from a different, already-recorded check instead of computing its own -- the sample size doesn't match what a genuine re-run would show. It has been superseded and is kept only as a documented record of the bug; it should not be treated as its own finding or pooled with anything else.

body_clock_night_dose_1400_1659.plain_summary: This entry was meant to test how a body-clock effect changes for games starting between 2:00 and 4:59 PM Eastern, but a data bug caused it to just copy the numbers from a different, already-recorded check instead of computing its own. It has been superseded and is kept only as a documented record of the bug; it should not be treated as its own finding or pooled with anything else.

body_clock_night_dose_1700_1959.plain_summary: This entry checks a body-clock effect for games starting between 5:00 and 7:59 PM Eastern, but only 3 games in the entire dataset ever fall into this narrow window, so there isn't remotely enough data to say anything -- it exists only to fill a complete ladder of kickoff-time buckets, not as a real result. It should not be interpreted at all.

body_clock_night_dose_ge2000.plain_summary: This entry checks a body-clock effect for games starting at or after 8:00 PM Eastern, using the exact same games and producing identical numbers to a separately named entry elsewhere in this registry -- it is kept only as a cross-reference pointer to that other result, not as independent evidence. It should not be pooled alongside anything else as if it were a separate finding.

body_clock_night_east_road_ge2000et.plain_summary: Control check: this looks at Eastern-time-zone road teams playing games starting at or after 8:00 PM Eastern -- late enough to exercise the same measurement method as the real West Coast body-clock checks, but not actually a body-clock mismatch for an Eastern-based team the way that kickoff time would be for a West Coast team. It behaved close to what was predicted going in, leaning toward a home advantage, but the sample is diluted by some Western-venue road games mixed in, so it works as a supporting instrument check rather than a standalone finding.

body_clock_night_west_road_ge2000et.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road for a true road game with a kickoff at 8:00 PM Eastern or later -- late in the evening for the Eastern-based home team, but still only mid-afternoon by the visiting team's own body clock. This was tested as a bet on that West Coast visiting team, on the idea that its body clock is actually working in its favor at that hour while the home team's is not, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, with roughly a 92% chance the effect ran in the predicted direction. It's closely related to other body-clock checks in this registry and should not be pooled with them as independent evidence.

body_clock_night_west_road_ge2000et_2009.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff at 8:00 PM Eastern or later, checked only in the 2009 through 2016 seasons. This was tested as a bet on that visiting team's favorable body-clock timing, and the limited data leaned toward the idea in that earlier era.

body_clock_night_west_road_ge2000et_2017.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff at 8:00 PM Eastern or later, checked only in the 2017 through 2025 seasons. This was tested as a bet on that visiting team's favorable body-clock timing, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, though more weakly than in the earlier era.

body_clock_night_west_road_true_slots.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road for a marquee prime-time game (Sunday, Monday, or Thursday night specifically, excluding games that start right around 7:00 PM Eastern). This narrower version of the late-kickoff body-clock check was tested as a bet on that visiting team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea; it overlaps heavily with a broader version of the same check elsewhere in this registry and should not be counted as independent evidence.

body_clock_west_host_east_visitor_late.plain_summary: Control check: a West Coast home team is hosting a visitor based in the Eastern time zone, with a kickoff at 7:00 PM Eastern or later -- a matchup where no body-clock advantage was expected for either side going in. It came back close to a coin flip as predicted, which supports the idea that this whole family of body-clock checks is measuring something real rather than just noise.

body_clock_west_road_early.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern -- about 10 or 11 in the morning by the visiting team's own body clock, unusually early for it to be playing a football game. This was tested as a bet on the home team, on the classic idea that an early body clock puts the traveling West Coast team at a disadvantage, and the limited data leaned toward the idea, though not strongly.

body_clock_west_road_early_2009_2016.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern, checked only in the 2009 through 2016 seasons. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and the limited data came back close to a coin flip in that earlier era.

body_clock_west_road_early_2017_2025.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff before 2:00 PM Eastern, checked only in the 2017 through 2025 seasons. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea more clearly than in the earlier era.

body_clock_west_road_midday_control.plain_summary: A Pacific or Arizona time-zone team is on the road with a kickoff between 2:00 and 4:59 PM Eastern -- a step later than the earliest kickoffs, used to check whether a body-clock disadvantage fades as the start time gets later in the day. This was tested as a bet on the home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea about as strongly as the earliest-kickoff version, not clearly weaker the way it would be expected to look if the effect faded smoothly with a later start time.

bye_overval_both_bye_sanity.plain_summary: Sanity check: both teams in this game are coming off a bye week at the same time, a rare situation used to make sure the bye-week detection method itself works correctly rather than to look for a betting edge. A bug in how bye weeks were detected (it could misdate a bye across a season boundary) was fixed shortly before this was recorded, and after the fix the result came back close to a coin flip, as expected for a sanity check.

bye_overval_fade_full_slate_post2011.plain_summary: Whichever team in a game is coming off a bye week (at least 12 days of rest) since the 2012 season, bet against that team, across every game in the league where this applies rather than only games where both teams are compared head to head. A bye-week-detection bug was fixed shortly before this was recorded, and after the fix the limited data leaned toward the idea, meaning the team with the extra rest covered somewhat less often than expected.

bye_overval_home_edge_post2011.plain_summary: The home team is coming off a bye week (at least 12 days of rest) while its opponent is not, since the 2012 season -- the idea that the betting market overrates the value of that extra rest and prices the home team too short. This was tested as a bet against that rested home team, and the limited data leaned toward the idea without being conclusive; it overlaps with a couple of other rest-and-milestone checks elsewhere in this registry and should not be pooled with them as independent evidence.

bye_overval_home_edge_pre2011.plain_summary: The home team is coming off a bye week while its opponent is not, checked only in the 2009 through 2011 seasons, before a labor-agreement change reportedly altered how real any bye-week rest advantage actually was. This slice is thin by construction (only 58 qualifying games), so it's meant to be read side by side with a larger, matching post-2011 version of the same check rather than on its own; the limited data here leaned toward the rested home team actually covering more, the opposite lean from the modern-era version.

bye_overval_road_fav_post2011.plain_summary: The visiting team is coming off a bye week and is favored by the betting market to win on the road, since the 2012 season -- a modern test of an old betting claim that road favorites coming off a bye cover roughly 73% of the time. The limited data here reads essentially null, giving no support to that old claim in the modern era.

cfb_bias_battery_bowl_eligibility_oppone.plain_summary: College football: a team's opponent needs just one more win to reach bowl-game eligibility (the standard six-win threshold), and it's week 8 or later in the season -- a motivated opponent fighting for a bowl spot. This check does not predict which side benefits going in; it's one of nineteen situational checks tried together in a batch on the same set of seasons, and the limited data leaned slightly toward the team facing that motivated opponent doing worse. A sign-and-scale correction was applied to this record after an earlier draft used the wrong, unscaled number, so the figure recorded here is the corrected one.

cfb_bias_battery_bowl_eligibility_self.plain_summary: College football: a team itself needs just one more win to become bowl-eligible (it has already won exactly 5 games), and it's week 8 or later in the season -- a spot where that team might be playing with extra motivation to lock in a bowl bid. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that motivated team leaned toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate.

cfb_bias_battery_bye_week_rest_edge.plain_summary: College football: a team has at least six more days of rest than its opponent, essentially a bye-week-sized rest advantage. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that better-rested team leaned toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate.

cfb_bias_battery_cfp_style_points_big_fa.plain_summary: College football: a team is favored by 21 points or more, late in the season (week 10 or later) in years since the College Football Playoff began, a spot where a ranked team might be trying to run up the score for playoff-committee 'style points.' Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, these heavy favorites leaned toward covering the spread less often than the rest of that week's slate, the opposite of what the style-points theory would predict.

cfb_bias_battery_eliminated_apathy.plain_summary: College football: a team has two wins or fewer entering week 10 or later, effectively out of realistic bowl contention -- the idea is that a team with nothing left to play for might not compete as hard. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that struggling team leaned strongly toward covering the spread less often than the rest of that week's slate, the most one-sided result in this batch of checks, though it's still one exploratory battery cell among many rather than a confirmed finding on its own.

cfb_bias_battery_heavy_public_favorite.plain_summary: College football: a team is favored by 17 points or more. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, these heavy favorites leaned slightly toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate, the opposite of the 'public overvalues big favorites' idea being tested.

cfb_bias_battery_high_altitude_road.plain_summary: College football: a visiting team is traveling to play at one of the sport's recognized high-altitude home venues. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, the data came back close to a coin flip, leaning only very slightly away from the idea that altitude hurts the visiting team's chances of covering.

cfb_bias_battery_letdown_after_upset_win.plain_summary: College football: a team pulled off a big road upset last week, winning outright as a 14-point underdog or more, the kind of result after which a team might be due for a motivational letdown. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that team leaned strongly toward covering the spread less often the following week than the rest of that week's slate, supporting the letdown idea.

cfb_bias_battery_mactic_short_prep_away.plain_summary: College football: a visiting team is playing a Tuesday or Wednesday night game, meaning less preparation time and a mid-week travel trip -- the kind of scheduling quirk some conferences use. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that traveling team leaned very strongly toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate, the opposite of what a short-prep-hurts-the-visitor idea would predict.

cfb_bias_battery_marquee_favorite_premiu.plain_summary: College football: one of the sport's biggest-name programs is favored to win. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, these marquee favorites actually leaned toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate, the opposite of the idea that the public overrates them and pushes their price too high.

cfb_bias_battery_marquee_underdog_value.plain_summary: College football: one of the sport's biggest-name programs is an underdog. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, the data came back essentially a coin flip, showing no real value in betting on a marquee program specifically when it's the underdog.

cfb_bias_battery_neutral_site_designated.plain_summary: College football: a game is being played at a neutral site, but the schedule still assigns one team the 'home' label for scheduling purposes even though neither team is actually playing at its own stadium. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, the designated 'home' side leaned very strongly toward covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate -- one of the more lopsided results in this batch of checks, though it is still one exploratory battery cell rather than a confirmed, independently tested finding.

cfb_bias_battery_off_big_ats_cover_carry.plain_summary: College football: a team covered the spread by 14 points or more last week, a hot streak that public bettors and the market might overreact to. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that team leaned toward covering the spread less often this week than the rest of that week's slate, consistent with the market overpricing a team coming off a big cover.

cfb_bias_battery_off_big_ats_miss_carryo.plain_summary: College football: a team missed covering the spread by 14 points or more last week, a bad miss that the market might overcorrect for by making that team too cheap to bet on this week. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that team leaned toward covering the spread less often this week too, the opposite of a bounce-back theory.

cfb_bias_battery_post_blowout_win_letdow.plain_summary: College football: a team won its previous game by 28 points or more, a blowout that might set up a letdown, or a 'trap game' against a weaker opponent, the following week. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that team leaned toward covering the spread less often the following week than the rest of that week's slate, supporting the letdown idea.

cfb_bias_battery_rivalry_finale_proxy.plain_summary: College football: this is the final regular-season game recorded for a team that season, often a rivalry-week finale. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch with no direction assumed in advance, teams in their season finale leaned very strongly toward covering the spread less often than the rest of that week's slate -- one of the more lopsided results in this batch of checks, though it is still one exploratory battery cell rather than a confirmed, independently tested finding.

cfb_bias_battery_short_week_rest_disadva.plain_summary: College football: a team has at least four fewer days of rest than its opponent heading into the game. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, that short-rested team leaned toward covering the spread less often than the rest of that week's slate.

cfb_bias_battery_state_quality_market_ga.plain_summary: College football: a team's measured on-field quality this season ranks much higher (at least 40 percentile points higher) than where the betting market's own spread ranks that team -- a case where the raw numbers say a team is better than the market seems to think. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch, this came back an almost exact coin flip, showing little sign that this quality-versus-market gap alone predicts covering the spread.

cfb_bias_battery_week2_overreaction_to_w.plain_summary: College football: it's week 2 of the season, and a team was involved in a blowout (a margin of 21 points or more, either way) in week 1 -- a case where the betting market might overreact to one small, early-season data point. Checked as one of 19 similar situational checks tried together in a single batch with no direction assumed in advance, that team leaned toward covering the spread less often in week 2 than the rest of that week's slate.

cfb_qb_dependence_interaction.plain_summary: College football: this tests adding a new ingredient to the prediction model -- how much value each team's starting quarterback creates per play, multiplied by how often that team throws the ball, added as an extra input alongside the model's existing stats. The underlying quarterback-value measurement itself is very consistent and repeatable from one half of the season to the other, but adding it to the model this way came back an almost exact coin flip for whether it actually improves predictions, and this result only concerns the college football version of the test -- a separate NFL version has not been run yet.

cfb_role_continuity.plain_summary: College football: this tests whether tracking how consistently the same players have been getting the ball (handoffs and pass targets) game to game, capped so a long streak doesn't dominate, adds anything to the prediction model beyond what it already uses. The underlying continuity measurement itself repeats reasonably well from one half of the season to the other, but adding it to the model leaned slightly toward hurting accuracy rather than helping, and this result reopens a related question about whether a similar idea could work across a different sport-to-sport comparison.

cfb_role_continuity_surgical_gate_direct.plain_summary: College football: not a bet on any game situation: this checks a technical question about how to build the previous participation-continuity feature -- specifically, whether only trusting it in games where the model's inputs already disagree with each other (a filtering technique) does better than using the feature everywhere without that filter. The limited data leaned toward the filtering technique helping, but this only says something about how to build that one feature, not whether the underlying idea beats the model's true baseline.

cfb_role_continuity_surgical_gated_vs_ba.plain_summary: College football: this tests the participation-continuity idea -- how consistently the same players have gotten the ball -- but only applying it in games selected by a specific filtering rule, compared directly against the model's true baseline with no continuity feature at all. The limited data leaned toward this filtered version hurting accuracy rather than helping, though it overlaps with two other closely related checks on the same games and shouldn't be treated as independent confirmation.

cfb_special_teams_punt_net_top_quartile.plain_summary: College football: a team ranked in the top quarter of the sport last season for net punting value (how much field position its punter earns after returns). Checked as a college-football replication of a similar NFL check, this leaned toward good-net-punting teams covering the spread more often than the rest of that week's slate -- notably, in the opposite direction from what the NFL version of this same check found, so the two sports disagree with each other here and neither result closes the question.

cfb_special_teams_return_top_quartile.plain_summary: College football: a team ranked in the top quarter of the sport last season for punt- and kickoff-return value. Checked as a college-football replication of a similar NFL check, this leaned toward good-return teams covering the spread less often than the rest of that week's slate -- the opposite direction from what the NFL version of this same check found, so the two sports disagree with each other here and neither result closes the question.
